summary.text: Positivity is proved by explicitly constructing a partition according to \(n \bmod 4\): \(\{n\}\), \(\{9,n-9\}\), \(\{18,n-18\}\), or \(\{27,n-27\}\), with the exceptional case \(n=27\) handled by \(\{27\}\). The variable part is divisible by \(4\), while \(9,18,27\) are divisible by \(9\), so every part has a nontrivial square divisor; the bound \(n>23\) ensures the parts are positive and distinct.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the number of partitions of \(n\) into distinct positive nonsquarefree parts. Equivalently, \(a(n)\) is the number of finite sets
\[
P\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots,n\}
\]
such that
\[
\sum_{k\in P}k=n
\]
and every \(k\in P\) is nonsquarefree. Using sets rather than lists automatically expresses the requirement that the parts be distinct.

We prove that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>23\) by explicitly constructing at least one such set \(P\).

First recall a simple criterion for nonsquarefreeness. A positive integer \(m\) is squarefree only if there is no integer \(d>1\) for which \(d^2\mid m\). Consequently:

* every multiple of \(4=2^2\) is nonsquarefree;
* \(9\), \(18\), and \(27\) are nonsquarefree, since each is divisible by \(9=3^2\).

Now fix \(n>23\). There are four cases according to the residue of \(n\) modulo \(4\).

**Case 1: \(n\equiv 0\pmod 4\).**

Take
\[
P=\{n\}.
\]
The sole part \(n\) is positive because \(n>23\), and of course \(n\le n\). Its sum is \(n\). Moreover, \(4\mid n\), so \(2^2\mid n\); hence \(n\) is nonsquarefree. Thus \(P\) is an admissible partition of \(n\).

**Case 2: \(n\equiv 1\pmod 4\).**

Since \(n>23\) and \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), we have \(n\ge25\). Take
\[
P=\{9,n-9\}.
\]
Both proposed parts are positive: \(9>0\), and \(n-9\ge16>0\). Both are at most \(n\). They are distinct, because equality \(9=n-9\) would imply \(n=18\), contradicting \(n>23\). Their sum is
\[
9+(n-9)=n.
\]
The part \(9\) is nonsquarefree because \(3^2=9\mid9\). Also,
\[
n-9\equiv1-9\equiv1-1\equiv0\pmod4,
\]
so \(4\mid n-9\). Therefore \(n-9\) is divisible by \(2^2\) and is nonsquarefree. Hence \(P\) is an admissible partition.

**Case 3: \(n\equiv 2\pmod 4\).**

Here \(n>23\) implies \(n\ge26\). Take
\[
P=\{18,n-18\}.
\]
The two parts are positive, since \(18>0\) and \(n-18\ge8>0\), and both are at most \(n\). They are distinct. Indeed, if \(18=n-18\), then \(n=36\), but \(36\equiv0\pmod4\), contrary to the assumption that \(n\equiv2\pmod4\). Their sum is
\[
18+(n-18)=n.
\]
The first part is nonsquarefree because \(9=3^2\mid18\). For the second part,
\[
n-18\equiv2-18\equiv2-2\equiv0\pmod4,
\]
so \(4=2^2\mid n-18\). Thus \(n-18\) is also nonsquarefree. Therefore this \(P\) is admissible.

**Case 4: \(n\equiv 3\pmod 4\).**

The smallest integer greater than \(23\) with this residue is \(27\), so we first handle \(n=27\). In that case take
\[
P=\{27\}.
\]
Its sum is \(27=n\), and its only part is positive and nonsquarefree because \(9=3^2\mid27\). Thus this is an admissible partition.

It remains to consider \(n\equiv3\pmod4\) with \(n\ne27\). Since the possible values above \(23\) are \(27,31,35,\ldots\), we then have \(n\ge31\). Take
\[
P=\{27,n-27\}.
\]
The parts are positive because \(27>0\) and \(n-27\ge4>0\), and both are at most \(n\). They are distinct: the second part is divisible by \(4\), because
\[
n-27\equiv3-27\equiv3-3\equiv0\pmod4,
\]
whereas \(27\equiv3\pmod4\), so it cannot equal \(n-27\). Their sum is
\[
27+(n-27)=n.
\]
Finally, \(27\) is nonsquarefree because \(9=3^2\mid27\), while \(n-27\) is nonsquarefree because it is divisible by \(4=2^2\). Hence this set is also an admissible partition.

In every possible residue class modulo \(4\), we have exhibited a finite set of distinct positive nonsquarefree integers whose sum is \(n\). This set is one of the partitions counted by \(a(n)\). Therefore the collection counted by \(a(n)\) is nonempty, and its cardinality satisfies
\[
a(n)>0.
\]
This proves the conjecture for every \(n>23\).
